mcq.prompt: Which statement about the half-open range `[first, last)` is correct?
choices: An empty range is expressed as first == last, and last must never be dereferenced
last denotes the final element, so *last is the last value in the range
An empty range is expressed as last < first
first and last may come from different containers as long as both are valid
mcq.explain: Excluding the upper endpoint is what removes the boundary special cases: emptiness is a plain equality test, std::distance(first, last) is the length, and any interior iterator splits the range cleanly. `last` is the one-past position, valid to hold and compare but never to dereference. Mixing endpoints from two containers violates the range precondition and is undefined behaviour, not a tolerated liberty.

mcq.prompt: Why does `std::ranges::find` work on a `std::forward_list` while `std::ranges::sort` does not?
choices: find is a range algorithm and sort is not
sort requires the elements to be copyable, and forward_list elements are not
find needs only input traversal, whereas sort needs random access to jump within the range
forward_list iterators cannot be compared for equality, which sort requires
mcq.explain: Iterator categories are capability tiers, and each algorithm names the weakest tier it can work with. A linear scan needs nothing beyond increment-and-read, so find accepts input iterators; sort partitions and recurses by moving to arbitrary positions, so it needs random access. Both have range forms — the constraint is the traversal capability, not the calling style, and forward iterators compare for equality perfectly well.

mcq.prompt: `std::ranges::sort(orders, [](const Order& l, const Order& r) { return l.price <= r.price; })` is called. What is the consequence?
choices: Equivalent orders are reversed, but the result is otherwise sorted
The call has undefined behaviour, because <= is not irreflexive and so is not a strict weak ordering
The sort becomes stable, since equal elements now compare true in both directions
It is merely slower, because equal elements are swapped needlessly
mcq.explain: compare(a, a) must be false; with <= it is true, so the comparator fails irreflexivity and the strict-weak-ordering precondition is violated. sort does not validate it — the manifestations reported in practice are a wrong order, an infinite loop, or an out-of-bounds write inside the library implementation, because the partition loop relies on the comparator to stop it. Stability is a property of stable_sort, not something a comparator can confer.

mcq.prompt: In `std::ranges::sort(orders, {}, &Order::price_ticks)`, what do the second and third arguments mean?
choices: An empty predicate meaning 'no filtering', and the member to sort into
A default-constructed allocator, and the key member
An empty tag selecting the classic overload, and a pointer used for stable tie-breaking
{} default-constructs std::ranges::less as the comparator, and &Order::price_ticks is a projection applied to each element before comparing
mcq.explain: Range algorithms take the comparator in the second slot and a projection in the third, so `{}` is simply the default std::ranges::less and the pointer-to-data-member maps each Order to its price before the comparison happens. That replaces the boilerplate two-parameter lambda and makes the compared key explicit at the call site. The projection changes what is compared, never what is stored or moved.

mcq.prompt: Orders arrive in time order and are sorted by price. Which algorithm keeps orders at the same price in their original arrival order?
choices: std::ranges::stable_sort
std::ranges::sort, since equivalent elements are never moved
std::ranges::sort with a comparator that also compares arrival time
std::ranges::partial_sort
mcq.explain: Two orders at the same price are equivalent under a price comparator — neither precedes the other — and sort is free to reorder an equivalence class, so time priority is lost. stable_sort preserves the prior relative order within each class by contract. Adding arrival time to the comparator does produce the same result here, but it changes the ordering itself rather than relying on stability, and it requires the tiebreaker key to exist in the element.

mcq.prompt: `std::ranges::binary_search(values, 3)` is called on an unsorted vector and returns the right answer during testing. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The call is fine; binary_search falls back to a linear scan when the range is unsorted
The call is fine for small ranges, where the search degenerates to a scan
The call violates its precondition and is undefined behaviour; one correct-looking result is not evidence that it is defined
The call is defined but unspecified, so it may return either answer
mcq.explain: The requirement is that the range be partitioned with respect to the comparator and the key — a range sorted under the same ordering satisfies it — and the library does not check. Violating it is undefined behaviour, not an unspecified choice among valid answers, and precondition bugs of this shape routinely survive debug tests and then surface under optimisation or on larger inputs.

mcq.prompt: `std::lower_bound` is called on a sorted `std::list`. What does its O(log N) guarantee actually promise?
choices: Logarithmic elapsed time, because the list nodes are traversed by pointer
Nothing, since lower_bound cannot be called on a bidirectional iterator
Logarithmic total work, since the standard counts every operation the algorithm performs
Logarithmically many comparisons; advancing a non-random-access iterator still costs O(N) steps overall
mcq.explain: The complexity guarantee is stated in comparisons, and on a list those really are logarithmic — but reaching each probe position requires walking nodes one at a time, so the call is linear in iterator movement. lower_bound is callable because forward traversal suffices; only the step count degrades. On a sorted vector both halves are cheap, which is the whole point of the flat-container pattern.

mcq.prompt: After `std::ranges::nth_element(orders, orders.begin() + 10, cmp)`, what is true of the range?
choices: The whole range is sorted, but only the first ten positions are guaranteed
The element at position 10 is where a full sort would put it, and the range is partitioned around it; neither side is ordered
The first ten elements are sorted and the tail is left untouched
The first ten elements are the ten largest, in descending order
mcq.explain: nth_element guarantees a rank and a partition, nothing more: everything before the selected position compares no greater than it and everything after compares no less, but the internal order of each side is unspecified. Reading its tail as though it were sorted is a plain logic bug. Sorting the ten-element prefix afterwards is exactly what turns the selection into a usable top-ten — that second step is not optional.

mcq.prompt: A million orders arrive and the caller needs the ten highest-priced ones, in order. Which is the cheapest correct approach?
choices: partial_sort onto a ten-element prefix, or nth_element followed by sorting that prefix — roughly O(N log 10) and average O(N) respectively
sort the whole range, then take the first ten — O(N log N) but simplest
sort the whole range with a parallel execution policy, then take the first ten
Repeatedly call max_element and erase, ten times
mcq.explain: Both selection algorithms avoid establishing an order among the 999,990 elements the caller will never read, which is an algorithmic reduction that dwarfs any instruction-level tuning of the full sort. partial_sort maintains a sorted K-prefix directly; nth_element does the selection in average linear time and then needs a ten-element sort to satisfy the 'in order' half of the requirement. Repeated max_element is O(K·N) with N erases on top.

mcq.prompt: What hidden cost does `std::stable_sort` carry that `std::sort` does not?
choices: It calls the comparator O(N²) times in the worst case
It requires the element type to be copyable rather than merely movable
It may allocate a temporary buffer, putting a heap operation inside an otherwise pure comparison-and-move call
It requires contiguous storage and so cannot be used on a std::deque
mcq.explain: Stability is achieved by merging, which wants scratch space: with a buffer stable_sort is O(N log N), and without one it falls back to roughly O(N log² N). The consequence for latency work is that a call which looks purely computational can reach the allocator. The comparison bound is never quadratic, and the same holds for stable_partition.

mcq.prompt: A sorted vector contains the price 101 three times. Which pair of iterators bounds exactly that run?
choices: [lower_bound(101), lower_bound(102))
[binary_search(101), upper_bound(101))
[lower_bound(100), upper_bound(101))
[lower_bound(101), upper_bound(101)), which equal_range returns as one half-open pair
mcq.explain: lower_bound gives the first element not less than the key and upper_bound the first element strictly greater, so together they delimit exactly the equivalent run, and equal_range computes both under one interface — returning a half-open pair that another algorithm can consume directly. binary_search returns only a bool and yields no position at all. The first option happens to coincide here only because the next distinct price is 102; it is not the general answer.

mcq.prompt: `auto at_or_above = std::ranges::lower_bound(orders, price); orders.insert(at_or_above, incoming);` — what must the code not do next?
choices: Assume the vector is still sorted; insertion at the lower bound breaks the ordering
Reuse at_or_above, because vector insertion invalidates iterators
Call lower_bound again, since the vector now needs re-sorting
Insert a second element, because a vector may only be inserted into once between sorts
mcq.explain: Inserting at the lower bound is exactly what keeps the vector sorted, so the ordering is fine — the hazard is the iterator, which is subject to std::vector's invalidation rules and is unusable after the insert whether or not a reallocation occurred. Recompute it if the position is needed again. Note also that each such insertion shifts a suffix; for a batch, appending everything and sorting once moves less data.

mcq.prompt: `auto cancelled = std::ranges::partition(orders, &WorkingOrder::active);` — what does `cancelled` denote?
choices: The subrange [partition point, end), whose beginning is the first element failing the predicate
An iterator to the first element satisfying the predicate
The subrange of elements satisfying the predicate
A pair of iterators bounding the elements that were moved
mcq.explain: The range form returns the second group as a subrange, so cancelled.begin() is the partition point: everything before it satisfies the predicate, everything from it on does not. That iterator is ordinary and composes with half-open algorithms — sorting orders.begin() to the partition point orders only the active ones after a single partitioning pass. partition_point recovers the same boundary later in logarithmically many predicate calls.

mcq.prompt: Which statement about `std::ranges::partition` and `std::ranges::partition_point` is correct?
choices: partition_point sorts the range first, so it works on any input
partition leaves both groups in their original relative order, so partition_point is redundant
partition_point requires the range to be already partitioned for the same predicate; on an arbitrary range its result is meaningless or undefined
partition_point is O(N) because it must apply the predicate to every element
mcq.explain: partition_point is a binary search over a Boolean property: it can be logarithmic precisely because it assumes all the true elements precede all the false ones. Hand it an unpartitioned range and it happily returns a wrong boundary — the same class of precondition failure as binary_search on unsorted data. Preserving relative order within each group is stable_partition's contract, which plain partition explicitly does not offer and which may cost a buffer allocation.

mcq.prompt: `std::accumulate(values.begin(), values.end(), 0)` is called over a `std::vector<double>`. What goes wrong, and where?
choices: Nothing; the result is converted to double on return
The call is ill-formed, because the initial value's type must match the element type
Only the final result is truncated, so a cast on the return value fixes it
The accumulator is an int, so every partial sum is truncated back to int inside the loop
mcq.explain: The initial value fixes both the accumulator type and the result type, so each addition produces a double that is immediately converted back to int before the next one — the loss compounds across the whole fold rather than happening once at the end. Casting the return value therefore cannot recover it; the fix is to pass 0.0, choosing an initial value of the intended accumulator type.

mcq.prompt: When is `std::reduce` an unsafe substitute for `std::accumulate`?
choices: Whenever the range is not contiguous, since reduce requires random access
Whenever the operation is not associative and commutative enough to tolerate regrouping — floating-point addition being the everyday example
Whenever the range contains more elements than the hardware thread count
Whenever the initial value is not the operation's identity element
mcq.explain: accumulate is a left fold in iterator order; reduce is permitted to regroup the operations, which is what enables vectorised or parallel evaluation. Integer addition without overflow tolerates that, but floating-point addition is not associative, so regrouping can change the rounded result and destroy run-to-run reproducibility. reduce also constrains the operation to accept combinations beyond (accumulator, element), which a directional operation may not support.

mcq.prompt: `std::ranges::transform(orders, std::back_inserter(quantities), &Order::quantity)` is called on an empty destination. Why does the chapter call `quantities.reserve(orders.size())` first?
choices: Because back_inserter grows the vector one push at a time, so without a reservation the destination reallocates repeatedly during the transform
Because transform requires the destination to have space before it will write anything
Because back_inserter is undefined behaviour on an empty container
Because reserve is what makes the output range sized, which transform requires
mcq.explain: An inserter is what lets transform write into a container that has no existing space, but each write is a push_back, so the destination goes through the usual geometric growth and the moves that come with it. Reserving once turns that into a single capacity decision. Writing into an existing range with a plain iterator is the other option, and that one really does require the space to be there already.

mcq.section: Heap, merge, set, and compaction algorithms
mcq.prompt: A deadline heap is stored in a `std::vector`. Which order of operations removes the selected extreme?
choices: vector::pop_back, then pop_heap to restore the heap property
pop_heap alone; it removes the element and shrinks the vector
pop_heap to move the extreme to the back and restore the heap in the preceding range, then vector::pop_back
make_heap, then vector::erase(begin())
mcq.explain: pop_heap swaps the extreme to the last position and re-establishes the heap invariant over everything before it; the container then destroys that last element with pop_back. Calling pop_back first would discard an arbitrary leaf rather than the selected deadline and leave the heap wrong. Algorithms never change a container's size — that division of labour is the same one behind remove_if plus erase.

mcq.section: Heap, merge, set, and compaction algorithms
mcq.prompt: `std::ranges::unique` is applied to a vector of ids that was never sorted. What is the outcome?
choices: Undefined behaviour, because unique requires a sorted range
The container shrinks to the distinct ids in their first-seen order
Nothing happens, because unique needs an explicit comparator for non-sorted input
Only runs of adjacent equal ids are coalesced, so scattered duplicates survive — a logic bug, not undefined behaviour
mcq.explain: unique only collapses *adjacent* equivalent elements, so on unsorted input it does something well-defined and useless. Sorting first is what makes equal ids adjacent and turns it into global deduplication. Note the second half of the idiom too: unique moves retained values forward and returns the leftover tail, but cannot change the container's size — the following erase is what actually removes the elements.

mcq.prompt: `auto result = std::ranges::find(make_values(), 15);` where make_values returns a `std::vector<int>` by value. What is the type of `result`?
choices: std::vector<int>::iterator, which dangles as soon as the statement ends
std::ranges::dangling, because the argument is a temporary non-borrowed range
std::optional<std::vector<int>::iterator>, empty when the value is absent
The call is ill-formed; range algorithms reject rvalue ranges
mcq.explain: The temporary vector is destroyed at the end of the full expression, so any iterator into it would be unusable the moment it was returned. Rather than hand back a guaranteed-dangling iterator, the range algorithms return std::ranges::dangling for a range that is not a borrowed_range, which turns a runtime lifetime bug into a compile error at the first attempt to use the result. A borrowed lvalue range gets the real iterator.

mcq.prompt: What does it mean to say that `orders | std::views::filter(p) | std::views::transform(f)` is lazy?
choices: The adaptors allocate no intermediate collection; the predicate and the transform run during iteration, one element pulled through all stages at a time
The predicate and the transform are each applied once and their results cached for later traversals
Each stage runs to completion over the whole range before the next stage begins
The work is deferred to a background thread and joined on first access
mcq.explain: Building the pipeline constructs a small composed object and does no element work; iteration then pulls a single order through filter and transform before advancing the source. What laziness does *not* mean is constant work: a filtered increment may test many source elements, and a second traversal recomputes every transform, because nothing was cached. Materialise with ranges::to when the results will be read more than once.

mcq.prompt: Why does a `std::views::filter` view generally not offer a constant-time `size()`?
choices: Because filter views are input ranges, which have no size at all
Because size() is only provided by views that own their elements
Because the count of accepted elements is unknown until the predicate has been run over the whole source
Because the source container's size may change under the view
mcq.explain: Answering size() would mean evaluating the predicate for every source element, which is exactly the O(N) work the view exists to defer, so the standard simply does not offer it. The practical consequence appears at materialisation: a sized source lets an implementation reserve the destination once, while a filtered source generally cannot, so the destination may grow as accepted elements arrive.

mcq.prompt: Which of these is the dangerous one?
choices: Passing an lvalue container to a function that builds and consumes a pipeline over it
Binding `auto buys = orders | std::views::filter(p);` where orders is a local vector used in the same scope
`get_orders() | std::views::filter(p)` consumed immediately, where get_orders returns by value
Returning `local | std::views::filter(p)` from a function, where local is a vector declared in that function
mcq.explain: A pipeline over an lvalue container keeps a reference-like upstream view, so returning it hands the caller a view onto a destroyed vector — the same lifetime disease as a dangling std::string_view. A pipeline directly over an rvalue container is safe, because views::all wraps the temporary in an owning_view that keeps the elements alive. Keeping the source in the receiving scope, as in the second and third options, is the ordinary correct pattern.

mcq.prompt: Which statement about standard execution policies is correct?
choices: par guarantees the algorithm runs on multiple threads, so the speedup is proportional to core count
The caller owns data-race freedom, and an exception escaping the algorithm causes std::terminate
The library synchronises side effects inside predicates and comparators automatically
par_unseq is the safest default because it gives the implementation the most freedom
mcq.explain: A policy is a permission, not a promise: the implementation may still run sequentially, while the caller has already accepted the semantic cost of allowing reordering and must keep the callbacks race-free itself. Escaping exceptions terminate. par_unseq is the most dangerous rather than the safest, because unsequenced execution forbids blocking operations — locking a mutex inside such a callback can deadlock.

mcq.prompt: A hot loop over a `std::vector<Order>` is rewritten as a `views::filter` pipeline. What is the most likely performance consequence?
choices: The filtered view is no longer a contiguous range, so contiguous-memory optimisations and vectorisation are blocked and each increment becomes a branchy scan
Nothing measurable, because the adaptor layers always inline away completely
The pipeline allocates an intermediate vector, adding one allocation per stage
The predicate is hoisted out of the loop, so the pipeline is strictly faster
mcq.explain: filter replaces a dense sweep with a predicate-driven search whose increment carries a data-dependent branch, and it strips the contiguous-range property even though the source is a vector — so the optimiser loses the guarantees it was using to vectorise and prefetch. The layers usually do inline, which is why the surviving cost is structural rather than call overhead. No intermediate container is created; that is what ranges::to is for.

reading.section: Heap, merge, set, and compaction algorithms
reading.explain: An algorithm sees iterators, never the container, so it cannot destroy anything: remove_if shuffles the three odd readings into the front and hands back the leftover tail, but the vector is still five elements long at the first print. distance over that returned subrange is 2 — the number of positions the survivors did not need. Only the erase changes the size, to 3. The tempting reading is that remove_if already removed something and size() is 3 twice over; the size a container reports is the container's business alone, which is exactly why this idiom has two halves.

The initial value is not just a type declaration, it is the first operand of the fold. Seeding a maximum with 0 means the answer can never drop below 0, so a day of pure debits reports a largest transaction of 0 — a value that is not in the input at all. The minimum is seeded with an actual element, so it correctly reports -900. Reading 0 as a harmless neutral start is the trap: it is only neutral for addition, and for max the identity would have to be the smallest representable int, which is why seeding from the first element (and rejecting an empty range up front) is the habit worth keeping.

The third argument is a projection and the second is the ordering itself, not a direction switch. max_element returns the element no other element compares *before* under the given ordering; with std::ranges::greater the ordering is reversed, so the element at the top of that ordering is the lowest score, cy at 17, and min_element under the same reversed ordering yields bo at 95. The tempting reading — greater means bigger, so max_element with greater is doubly the maximum — inverts the comparator twice in the reader's head and once in the code. Either keep the default ordering and swap the algorithm, or keep the algorithm and swap the ordering, never both.

Integer division truncates before the offset, so the three readings map to 35, 39 and 42 and each pass sums to 116; the two passes agree because the transform is a pure function of its input. What they do not share is the work: nothing is memoised, so the lambda runs once per element per traversal and the counter reaches 6. The tempting reading is that laziness caches — that building `fahrenheit` computed the values once, or that the second loop reuses the first. Lazy means no output container is allocated and no work happens until you iterate; it says nothing about repeating that work on the next iteration, which is the argument for materialising with ranges::to when a pipeline is read twice.

upper_bound answers with the first position strictly greater than the key, so a newcomer lands after every ticket already at its priority and the queue stays first-in-first-out within each priority band. Tracing: a gives [2a]; b goes to the front; c goes after 2a; d goes after 1b. The tempting reading is that lower_bound and upper_bound differ only for a key that is present and are therefore interchangeable here — but a key that is present is precisely what a priority queue has, and lower_bound would insert *before* the equals, printing 1d 1b 2c 2a and quietly giving the newest ticket priority over the oldest.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: The vector returned by read_config_keys is a temporary that dies at the end of the full expression, so an iterator into it would be dead before it could be used. A std::vector is not a borrowed_range, so ranges::find deduces its return type as std::ranges::dangling — a type with no operator*, no operator-> and no conversion to an iterator — and the member access through it is what fails to compile. The tempting reading is that the temporary lives as long as `found` refers to it; nothing here extends its lifetime, and the library's answer is to make the mistake unrepresentable rather than to hand back an iterator that dangles at runtime. Bind the vector to a named variable first, or finish the search in the same expression.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: The two endpoints must describe one sequence. Here they name positions in two unrelated allocations, so the loop increments monday's iterator looking for equality with tuesday's end — a comparison that never has to become true — and keeps reading past the end of monday's buffer, which the address sanitizer reports as a heap-buffer-overflow. It compiles because both endpoints have the same type; the iterator model has no way to check that they belong together. The tempting reading is that this is at worst a wrong count, since the two vectors are 'next to each other' in the source; there is no such adjacency in memory, and counting both days means two calls added together.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: Inserting at the lower bound is the correct way to keep the vector sorted, so the container is fine; the iterator is not. The vector's size equals its capacity, so the insert reallocates, and `at` still points into the old buffer that the vector has already freed — the read is a heap-use-after-free the sanitizer flags. The tempting reading is that the value is still 30 either way, so the print is harmless; a stale iterator is invalid regardless of what happens to be behind it, and vector::insert invalidates iterators at or after the insertion point whether or not it reallocated. Capture insert's return value, which is a valid iterator to the newly inserted element.

writing.prompt: A speedrun leaderboard holds `Entry{std::string handle; int score; int seconds;}`. Write `rank(std::vector<Entry>&)` that orders it by score descending, then by seconds ascending, then by handle ascending. The contract: exactly one call to a sorting algorithm, one comparator, and the comparator must be a strict weak ordering — argue for that in a comment rather than asserting it.
checklist: A single sort call with a single comparator; no repeated passes over different keys
Score is compared in the reverse direction from seconds and handle within that one comparator
Every comparison uses < (or >), never <= or >=
Comment argues irreflexivity and transitivity, e.g. via the lexicographic tuple comparison
The comparator takes both parameters by const reference
writing.notes: Two sorts -- by handle, then by score -- is the classic wrong answer: the second sort is unstable and is free to scramble the first. Two *stable* sorts in reverse key order does work, but it costs a second pass and a possible buffer allocation to express what one comparator says directly. Because the comparator is a total tie-break, stability is irrelevant here: no two distinct entries are equivalent unless all three keys match.

writing.prompt: Write `median(std::vector<double> samples, double fallback)` for a sensor stream. It takes the vector by value and may reorder it. Contract: average linear time — the range must never be fully sorted — correct for both odd and even sizes, and `fallback` is returned for an empty input.
checklist: Empty input returns fallback before any iterator arithmetic
Uses nth_element (not sort or partial_sort) for the selection
The even case averages the two middle values, not one of them
The second middle value is found with max_element over the left partition, not by sorting it
A comment states that nth_element leaves both sides unordered but partitioned
writing.notes: Sorting and indexing the middle is the obvious O(N log N) answer and is the right call for a handful of samples; the point of the exercise is that the ordering of the other N-1 elements is work nobody reads. Note also that median of an even-sized set is a definition choice: averaging the two central values is the common one, but a latency histogram usually wants a named percentile rule instead.

writing.prompt: `starts` holds appointment start times in minutes, sorted ascending, with duplicates allowed. Write `count_in_window(const std::vector<int>& starts, int from, int until)` returning how many appointments start in the half-open window `[from, until)`. Contract: logarithmic in the size of the vector — no call may inspect every element.
checklist: Uses two binary searches, not count_if or any linear scan
The lower edge is inclusive and the upper edge exclusive: lower_bound is used for both
The result is a distance between the two iterators, not a Boolean or an index
The second search is bounded by the first iterator, not by starts.begin()
A comment or the signature makes the sorted-input precondition explicit
writing.notes: Using upper_bound for the upper edge would include appointments starting exactly at `until`, turning the window closed -- the kind of off-by-one that only shows up on a boundary-aligned query. If the window edges are themselves keys of a different type from the elements, the projection parameter is what keeps the comparison honest without writing a heterogeneous comparator.

writing.prompt: A build plan is a `std::vector<Step>` where `Step` has `std::string name` and `bool ready`. Write `hoist_ready(std::vector<Step>&)` that moves every ready step ahead of every blocked one and returns the number of ready steps. Contract: the relative order *within* each group must be exactly what it was — a build log has to stay readable — and the function must not sort.
checklist: Uses stable_partition, not partition and not sort
Passes &Step::ready as the projection or an equivalent predicate
Derives the count from the returned subrange's begin(), not by counting ready steps again
The returned count is computed as a distance from steps.begin()
A comment notes that stable_partition may allocate a temporary buffer
writing.notes: The boundary is an ordinary iterator, so `[steps.begin(), blocked.begin())` composes directly with any half-open algorithm -- sorting or printing just the ready steps needs no further searching. If the plan were re-partitioned later with the same predicate, partition_point recovers the boundary in logarithmically many predicate calls, but only because the range is already partitioned for it.

writing.prompt: A shopping basket is stored as two parallel arrays: `std::span<const std::int32_t> unit_price_cents` and `std::span<const std::int32_t> quantities`. Write `basket_total` returning the total in cents as `std::int64_t`. Contract: one pass, no intermediate container, mismatched lengths rejected rather than silently truncated, and no product may be computed in 32-bit arithmetic.
checklist: Rejects mismatched span sizes explicitly instead of using the shorter one
Uses transform_reduce (or inner_product) over both ranges; no temporary vector is built
The initial value is std::int64_t{0}, not 0
The widening cast is applied to an operand before the multiplication, not to the product
A comment states that signed overflow is undefined behaviour, not a wrap
writing.notes: transform_reduce is permitted to regroup its additions, which is exactly why it can vectorise -- harmless for integer addition that does not overflow, and unacceptable if these were doubles and the total had to reproduce bit for bit. In that case accumulate's ordered left fold is the one with the guarantee you need.

writing.section: Heap, merge, set, and compaction algorithms
writing.prompt: Two sorted, duplicate-free manifests of file paths describe last night's build and tonight's. Write `merge_manifests` returning every path that appears in either, sorted and with no path twice, and `only_tonight` returning the paths added since last night. Contract: neither function may sort, and neither may use an associative container.
checklist: Both functions use a sorted-set algorithm (set_union and set_difference)
Neither calls sort, unique, or any container with its own ordering
Output is produced through back_inserter into a vector, or into a sized destination
merge_manifests reserves against a stated bound before writing
A comment states the shared-ordering precondition on both inputs
writing.notes: Argument order is the whole meaning of set_difference: swapping the two ranges answers the opposite question -- what disappeared -- and the compiler has nothing to say about it. std::ranges::merge is the other tool here; it keeps every element from both inputs, so a path present in both would appear twice, which is why set_union rather than merge answers this contract.

writing.prompt: Given `const std::vector<int>& samples` in arrival order, write `print_recent_spikes(samples, threshold)` that prints the three most recent readings above the threshold, newest first, one per line. Contract: no container may be created, the samples must not be copied or reordered, and the scan must stop as soon as three spikes have been printed rather than walking the whole history.
checklist: Builds one pipeline and iterates it; no vector, no ranges::to, no copy of samples
Reverses before filtering so that 'most recent' is what take bounds
take(3) bounds the output, and fewer than three spikes is handled by the pipeline itself
The parameter is a const reference and no element is modified
A comment explains that iteration pulls one element through all stages, so the scan stops early
writing.notes: Filtering before reversing would produce the same three numbers, because reversing a filtered range still yields the last three accepted elements -- but it forces the filter to be traversed from its far end, and reverse over a filter_view is the awkward composition to reason about. Note that `recent` refers to the caller's vector: it must not be returned or stored, only consumed here.

writing.prompt: An offline log analysis counts HTTP status codes of 400 and above over a `std::span<const std::uint32_t>` holding hundreds of millions of entries. Write `count_rejects` that uses a parallel execution policy where the library provides one and compiles unchanged where it does not. Contract: the predicate must be safe under the policy you choose, and a comment must say why this call belongs offline rather than on a request path.
checklist: The <execution> include is guarded, so the file compiles where the header is absent
The parallel call itself is guarded by a feature-test macro such as __cpp_lib_parallel_algorithm
The fallback branch calls the same algorithm with no policy argument
The predicate is pure: no shared counter, no locking, no I/O
A comment names scheduling overhead or loss of core placement as the reason to keep it offline
writing.notes: par_unseq would additionally allow the calls to be interleaved within one thread, which forbids anything that blocks -- a mutex taken inside such a predicate can deadlock against itself. Note also that policies are arguments to the classic algorithms, not to std::ranges, and that an exception escaping a policy-taking call is not propagated: the implementation calls std::terminate.
